title: Why it's never too early to start with sales · hancrafted
description: Why sales must start long before revenue is needed, and the first concrete steps to build a sales pipeline: find your zero-cash month, keep a list of potential customers, make first contact, and track your conversion rate and sales cycle.

slides.text: Why it's never too early to start with sales Revenue arrives months after the costs that create it, so by the time you feel you need sales it is already too late: start the pipeline before you need the money.
Why watching cashflow is mission critical

01 · Why watching cashflow is mission-critical Watch your cashflow A million euros is coming, and the company is gone. Your turn If February is the month you run out, when would you have needed to start selling? Jan Cash €100,000 Cost −€50,000 Cash €50,000 Cash left €50,000 Feb Cash €50,000 Cost −€50,000 Cash €0 Cash left €0 March Cost −€50,000 Cash left −€50,000 April Revenue €1,000,000 Cash left €950,000 Bankrupt Two months of cash The million lands one month late
Why sales is more than just selling

Three payouts before revenue Sales is more than selling Selling early pays out three times, and all three arrive before the revenue does . Gain market insight plus gain internal insights equals increase trust. 01 Gain market insight Every customer talk is research you did not pay for. When did this last happen to you? Last month. We lost two days on it. Where to spend your time Hypothesis 2 A network 02 Gain internal insights How well do you sell, and could anyone besides you repeat it? You repeat it first sales hire a team 03 Increase trust Investors and reluctant customers trust what someone else has already bought. Before revenue What 885 VCs weigh most Team 95% Business model 83% Product 74% Market 68% Attracting investment Convincing reluctant customers What you learn The "=" is a claim, not a proof: a first result shows your team can sell. Survey of 885 institutional venture capitalists: Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev, How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions?
Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time

One board, three readings What is a sales pipeline The columns are your funnel, the drop between them is your conversion rate, and the way across is your sales cycle. Conversion rate 3 : 1 How many leads become one opportunity: tells you your offering Sales funnel the stages, and how many sit in each: tells you your volume Lead 6 Kraus Bakery Novak Dental Hofmann Logistics Brightline Studio Okafor & Co Lindqvist Tools Opportunity 2 Kraus Bakery demo booked Novak Dental proposal sent Deal 1 Novak Dental €12,000 signed, invoice in 30 days Sales cycle · first contact to the money: tells you your efficiency

Count the notes Pipeline by the numbers Do you have 27 names? That is what one deal takes in this example, 9.5 months before the money. 27 : 1 total conversion: 27 leads for 1 deal Lead · 27 2 weeks Kraus Novak Hahn Okafor Lind Meyer Santos Petrov Weber Dubois Haas Larsen Moretti Fischer Ito Becker Nowak Schulz Rossi Keller Varga Bauer Jansen Wolf Costa Sato Ahmed 3:1 Opportunity · 9 6 months Kraus demo Novak proposal Weber pricing Haas demo Fischer legal Nowak proposal Keller demo Bauer pricing Sato demo 9:1 Deal · 1 3 months Novak €12,000 signed 8 others still talking or lost Sales cycle: 9.5 months from first lead to money 2 wk Opportunity · 6 months Deal · 3 months → money

Your board on day one Why it takes time to ramp up Nothing is written yet: no material, only questions about the market, and the two numbers you plan with are blank. 1 · Preparation Before Sales deck · Pricing · Offering · Business model During Demo · Meeting slides · Proposal Deal Contract · Compliance · Legal dashed: not written yet 2 · Unknown market Who is really your customer? What are they willing to pay? What problem do they really need solved? answered only by real conversations 3 · Unknown metrics Conversion rate ? : 1 Sales cycle ? months Both needed to plan backwards from your cash. Day one Each column shrinks only by doing. How many of these three have you started?

Watch your cashflow Costs begin before customers Company setup and the founders' living costs arise before a startup has users or income. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, A Student's Guide to Startups: Startup Funding ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com A high burn rate is a clock It puts a startup under constant time pressure, and the stated remedy is to spend little while working fast. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, A Student's Guide to Startups: Startup Funding ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com The default-alive test Ask whether the company reaches profitability on its remaining money at current expenses and growth; worrying too early is cheap, worrying too late is dangerous. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Default Alive or Default Dead? ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com
Why sales is more than just selling No speaker notes for this Slide.

Sales is more than selling Your starting model is wrong A founder's initial model of users is always inaccurate, even when the founder is one of them, and direct contact with the earliest users gives the best feedback the company will get. 1 Sources (1) Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com Ask about the last time What yields insight is specifics: ask about problems the user already faced, not hypotheticals, and treat talking to customers as part of the CEO's job. 1 The sources are interviews and users, not sales calls; that a sales conversation yields the same facts is an inference. Sources (1) Y Combinator (Migicovsky), Startup School Week 1 Recap: How to Talk to Users ( opens in a new tab ) ycombinator.com A signal must be costly to fake When one side knows more than the other, an action that is cheaper for a strong type than a weak one carries information, because the cost carries it, not the content. 1 Sources (1) Spence, Job Market Signaling ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Investors read the team In a survey of 885 institutional venture capitalists the management team was the most-cited factor (95%), ahead of business model (83%), product (74%) and market (68%). 1 Sources (1) Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev, How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? ( opens in a new tab ) nber.org No study measures LOIs or pipelines Carrying signaling theory over to early sales results is an inference, and a non-binding letter of intent is cheap to give, so it separates strong from weak firms poorly; the more binding the commitment, the more trust it plausibly earns. 1 Sources (1) Spence, Job Market Signaling ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Premature scaling burns cash Blank calls premature scaling of sales and marketing the leading cause of cash loss in a startup. 1 Sources (1) Blank, It Must Be A Marketing Problem ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com Friends' orders can mislead Early orders from board members or friends are good for morale and cash but may not show what the business model is. 1 Sources (1) Blank, It Must Be A Marketing Problem ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com

What is a sales pipeline Stage rates are not portable A stage's rate depends on where a vendor draws its start and end, so rates from different companies are likely not comparable stage by stage; in one dataset two stages already differ, 68 and 19 percent. This is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com Cycle length hits cash A unit-economics model leaves out the sales cycle and the ramp time of a salesperson; their effect on cash flow has to be modelled separately 1 . Sources (1) Mark Roberge, The Science of Scaling ( opens in a new tab ) f.hubspotusercontent10.net

Pipeline by the numbers A reference win rate In a dataset of 655 thousand opportunities across 387 companies, the new-customer win rate was 19 percent (about 5.3 opportunities per win), the sales cycle 91 days and 8 stakeholders per deal; expansion sales to existing customers ran 45 percent, 52 days and 5 stakeholders. It is a vendor study of its own customers' CRM data 1 . Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com The biggest loss is no decision An analysis of more than 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found 40 to 60 percent of deals are lost to buyers who intend to buy but never act 1 . Sources (1) Dixon and McKenna, Stop Losing Sales to Customer Indecision (Harvard Business Review) ( opens in a new tab ) hbr.org Everyone holds a veto Sellers rarely find one person who can approve a deal alone; decision authority rests with a group whose members have different roles and all have veto power 1 . Sources (1) Schmidt, Adamson and Bird, Making the Consensus Sale (Harvard Business Review) ( opens in a new tab ) hbr.org Buying groups disagree A Gartner survey of 632 B2B buyers describes buying groups of five to 16 people; 74 percent of teams showed unhealthy conflict, and groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal 1 . Sources (1) Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate "Unhealthy Conflict" During The Decision Process ( opens in a new tab ) gartner.com

Why it takes time to ramp up Startups search, they do not execute Established companies execute a business model, a startup is a temporary organization designed to search for a repeatable and scalable one 1 . Sources (1) Steve Blank, The Customer Development Manifesto ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com Selling blind In one case, early orders from industry friends and board connections covered the first months of the revenue plan but did not show why customers would buy, because nobody had run customer discovery 1 . Sources (1) Steve Blank, It Must Be A Marketing Problem ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com Learn first, codify later Before product-market fit, rely on personal networks and customer referrals: they do not scale but yield the best opportunities to learn from. Codify the playbook after that learning and prove the unit economics before hiring salespeople aggressively 1 . Sources (1) Mark Roberge, The Science of Scaling ( opens in a new tab ) f.hubspotusercontent10.net Metrics lag by one cycle A conversion figure for recent leads looks worse than its long-run value because those leads have not yet gone through a full cycle; older results are the better estimate 1 . Sources (1) Mark Roberge, The Science of Scaling ( opens in a new tab ) f.hubspotusercontent10.net

Why watching cashflow is mission critical 0:00 – 0:23 Imagine the wall Imagine you are the founder, standing in front of one wall. Sticky notes, one column per month, yellow for the cash you have, red for the costs, green for the revenue. You have watched a board like this, or you are about to, and you know the feeling when you read the last column. 0:23 – 0:42 Cash decides how long you have Here is the claim of this whole Episode: what decides how long your company lives is not how much you earn in the end, but when the money arrives. This one board comes back three times, and each time it answers a bigger question. 0:42 – 0:58 The route We will go through four questions. Why cashflow is mission critical, why sales is more than selling, how to start doing sales, and why a pipeline takes time to build. The first answer is already on the wall.

Watch your cashflow 0:00 – 0:14 Walk the months Read it with me. January, you start with 100 thousand in cash and 50 thousand goes out. February, another 50 thousand goes out, and at the end of February your cash is zero. 0:14 – 0:24 March has no money March arrives and the cost lands on an empty account, with nothing to pay it. The big number sits in April, one month late. 0:24 – 0:32 Antithesis A million euros is coming, and the company is gone. Right on paper, dead on the calendar. 0:32 – 0:44 Hand over the verdict So find your own February: the month your cash hits zero. And if that is the month you run out, when would you have needed to start selling?

Why sales is more than just selling 0:00 – 0:15 Pain first You may think sales is something for later, when the money is needed. If so, you leave most of its value on the table, because the money is the last thing sales gives you. 0:15 – 0:25 The claim My claim is this: selling early pays out before the revenue does. There are three payouts, and each one is a reason to start now.

Sales is more than selling 0:00 – 0:17 Every talk is research Every customer conversation is market research you did not have to pay for. It tells you where to spend your time and which hypothesis to drop. This is my reading of selling as a conversation, not a measured result. 0:17 – 0:31 Know how well you sell The second payout stays inside your company. You learn how well you sell, and whether anyone besides you could repeat it, because a repeatable process is what lets you hire the first salesperson. 0:31 – 0:49 Trust is the sum The third is trust. Investors and reluctant customers trust what someone else has already bought. To be straight about it, that is a claim and not a proof: a first result shows that your team can sell, and that is why it counts. 0:49 – 1:00 Verdict Insight and process both end in trust, so look at the three boxes and ask yourself which one your next investor would ask about first.

How to start doing sales 0:00 – 0:16 Backward chaining Start from the end and walk backwards. The end is a signed contract, and you walk back until the next step is in your own hands, because do sales is too vague to start on a Monday. 0:16 – 0:28 The claim Here is the claim: sales has three stages, leads, opportunities and closing. The first steps are ones you control, and only after them does it become a numbers game. 0:28 – 0:39 Signposting We go left to right. First the stages, then a deal board to track them, then marketing, and then the cashflow board once more.

Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time 0:00 – 0:10 The obvious objection So the obvious objection: I start selling in January, and the April revenue lands in March? It does not work like a switch. 0:10 – 0:19 The claim A pipeline is built, measured and tuned, and that takes months. Three words describe it: funnel, conversion rate and sales cycle.

What is a sales pipeline 0:00 – 0:10 Funnel is volume The funnel names each stage of your sales process. How many enter each stage tells you how much volume you can put through. 0:10 – 0:26 Conversion is the offer The conversion rate says how many actions in a stage become one success in the next. A low rate may be telling you that your offering is not yet attractive, and that is useful to know early. 0:26 – 0:40 Cycle is efficiency The cycle is the time from start to finish, until the deal or the money. It is your efficiency, and with conversion that gives you two numbers you should measure from your first deal.

Pipeline by the numbers 0:00 – 0:11 Read the picture Read the picture. Lead to opportunity is three to one, opportunity to deal is nine to one, so together it takes 27 leads for one deal. 0:11 – 0:24 Read the clock Now read the clock. Two weeks, six months, three months, which makes 9.5 months from first lead to money. Think one step further and ten deals need 270 leads. 0:24 – 0:37 Backward chain So chain it backwards. If you want a deal in month X, count back 9.5 months, and by then you need 27 names in the funnel. Do you have 27 names? 0:37 – 0:50 Your numbers, not mine One thing I want to be straight about: this is my worked example, not a law. Yours will be shorter or longer, which is exactly why you measure your own.

Why it takes time to ramp up 0:00 – 0:15 Preparation The first box is preparation. Before, during and at the deal you need a deck and pricing, a demo and a proposal, a contract and the legal side. None of that exists on day one. 0:15 – 0:27 Unknown market The second is an unknown market. Who is your customer, what do they pay, which problem really hurts. Only real conversations answer that, and desk research will not. 0:27 – 0:42 Unknown metrics The third is unknown metrics. You have no conversion rate and no cycle length yet, and you need both to plan backwards from your cash. How many months this takes, I will not invent for you. 0:42 – 0:54 So start now So start now, because each box shrinks only by doing. How many months do you have left, and how many of these three boxes have you started?

Start before you need the money 0:00 – 0:07 Back to the wall Back to the wall, one last time, with the answer to the question we opened with. 0:07 – 0:14 Peak-end close I will close with the four steps, one honest caveat and a small offer. Here they come.
